subtype: Approach: do nothing because it is not my job [Pitfall]
passage:
Chidi saw the mismatch on his second week at the firm in Manchester: three payments that did not line up with the delivery sheets. He mentioned it to Jamal, the analyst at the next desk, who shrugged. "Someone above us must have seen it. It isn't our job."

Chidi nodded, relieved. Raising it might make him look like a rookie hunting for trouble, and his probation review was coming. He turned back to his own work.

Six months later the same gap had grown into a dozen entries. When the external team asked who had checked the sheets, Chidi's initials were on the working papers. Jamal said he'd assumed Chidi had handled it, and Chidi realised they had each thought the other would speak.

qa.q: What did Jamal say when Chidi mentioned the payments?
qa.a: Jamal said that someone above them must have seen it and that it was not their job.

qa.q: Why did Chidi feel relieved after Jamal's answer?
qa.a: Chidi was worried about looking like a rookie before his probation review, so being told it was not his job excused him from the risk.

qa.q: What could Chidi have done in the second week instead, and why?
qa.a: Chidi could have quietly asked his supervisor whether the payments were already known, because a simple question checks the assumption without accusing anyone.

qa.q: How does Jamal see the situation when the external team asks questions?
qa.a: Jamal thought Chidi had handled it, so Jamal sees a shared silence in which each person assumed someone else was responsible.

grounding: A person tells themselves the problem is not their job and others must know, and the problem grows.

subtype: Approach: do nothing because it is not my job [Pitfall]
passage:
In the purchase department of a Pune hospital, Naveen noticed in his first month that the bandage supplier's invoices were always for more boxes than stores received. The gap was small each time.
He mentioned it once to Tushar at the next desk. Tushar shrugged. 'Everyone's seen it. If it mattered, someone senior would've fixed it.'
That made sense to Naveen. He was new. Raising it might mark him as a troublemaker before his confirmation. Surely audit knew. Surely his manager knew. He stopped looking at those invoices closely.
Eight months later, internal audit found the gap had grown every month, into lakhs, and the supplier had also been short-supplying sterile dressings to the wards. Stores was told to count every delivery from that day. In the review meeting the auditor asked the team, 'Did anyone notice this?'
Naveen looked at Tushar. Tushar looked at the floor. Five people had noticed. Nobody had said anything, because each thought someone else would.

qa.q: What did Tushar say when Naveen mentioned it?
qa.a: 'Everyone's seen it. If it mattered, someone senior would've fixed it.'

qa.q: Why did Naveen stop looking at the invoices closely?
qa.a: He felt too new and was afraid of being marked a troublemaker, and reassured himself that others must already know.

qa.q: What could Naveen have done in his first month?
qa.a: Written down what he saw and raised it quietly with his manager or the ethics channel, instead of assuming someone else would.

qa.q: How might the auditor feel hearing that five people had noticed?
qa.a: Frustrated and dismayed that a small gap grew for eight months because each person waited for someone else.

grounding: Shows a new employee telling himself others must know and that speaking up would hurt his career, while the problem grows.

subtype: Approach: do nothing because it is not my job [Pitfall]
passage:
Dear Vasudha ma'am,
You once told our ethics class that 'someone should do something' usually means nobody will. I'm writing because I've just learned what you meant.
At the logistics company, in my first month, I noticed that the fuel bills for two trucks were far higher than their routes could explain. I asked a senior; he said the supervisor surely knew. The supervisor was friendly with the drivers. I told myself it wasn't my job, and that speaking up could cost me my confirmation. Three other juniors saw the same thing. We joked about it once over tea, and did nothing.
This month audit found it had been going on for a year and had spread to five trucks. In the meeting the manager asked, 'Why did nobody report this?' None of us answered.
I'm not writing for comfort. I'm writing to say I understand now, and next time I'll be the one who speaks first, through the proper channel.
With respect,
Akash

qa.q: How many trucks were affected by the time audit found it?
How does Akash feel writing this letter?
qa.a: Ashamed and regretful about staying silent, but determined to act differently next time.

qa.q: What could Akash and the other juniors have done in the first month?
qa.a: One of them could have written down the fuel figures and reported them through the proper channel, instead of assuming the supervisor knew.

qa.q: How might Vasudha ma'am feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Saddened by what happened but moved that the lesson finally landed, and hopeful about what Akash will do next time.

grounding: Shows new employees each assuming others knew and staying silent to protect their careers, while the problem spreads.
